events.title: Forbidden Pages: Past and Present
events.description: Forbidden Pages: Past and Present features books, periodicals, photographs, and other materials from the USC Libraries’ collections that tell the story of censorship and resistance over the centuries. Among them are a charred fragment of Lion Feuchtwanger’s novel Jud Süß, pulled from the embers of the Nazi book burnings in Berlin in 1933; a 1761 edition of the Catholic Church’s Index Librorum Prohibitorum, its centuries-long list of prohibited books; and a 1954 issue of ONE Magazine which the Los Angeles postmaster declared obscene and refused to mail. Visitors will also encounter works by authors ranging from John Milton, Harriet Beecher Stowe, and Mark Twain to Toni Morrison, Judy Blume, and Salman Rushdie. The exhibition opens on Monday, October 5, in Doheny Memorial Library’s first-floor and runs through the fall semester. Presented in partnership with the USC Open Dialogue Project.

events.title: Amanda Flowers: Cosmic Nexus of The Soul • Soil | MFA Art Solo Thesis Exhibition
events.description: Opening reception: Thursday, November 5, 6 – 9 pm Exhibition on view: November 5 – 20, 2026 Gallery hours: Tuesday – Sunday, 11am – 5pm Roski Graduate Gallery (Los Angeles Arts District) 1262 Palmetto St, Los Angeles, CA 90013 More information here: https://roski.usc.edu/amanda-flowers/ ABOUT THE EXHIBITION Interdisciplinary artist Flowers explores the hidden communication and connection with our living planet through the practice of secret and sacral tools historically used in the preservation of Black ancestral linkage. Moving through an expansive language of identification she implements numerology, metaphysics, and spiritual mythologies, developing her own visual vernacular termed “Leavings.” Cumulatively, her practice embodies a site to dissect the duality of herself, a safe haven to sift through repressed energy. She creates a fragmented code from the threads of primordial dreamscapes to the cosmos, and in so doing a broader consideration of what makes a reflexive state. ABOUT THE ARTIST Amanda Flowers (b. 1995) is an interdisciplinary artist from the Bay Area, based in Los Angeles. Flowers initially attended Arizona State University to study astrophysics before rediscovering her passion for painting and returning home to pursue art in 2015. She later moved to Los Angeles, where she became immersed in the entertainment industry while developing her practice as an emerging artist. In 2023, Flowers received her BA in Studio Art from California State University, Los Angeles. Flowers’s work draws from her dreams, inherited familial memories, and imagined terrains of the “The Shadow Realm.” Her practice is deeply informed by the journey of her maternal grandparents, who migrated from North Carolina during the Great Migration in the late 1960s. Through envisioned ancestral motifs, she creates bridges between generations honoring her lineage. Drawing from a constellation of Black spiritual traditions and mythologies, Flowers moves between the emotional subconscious, the metaphysical and material histories of Black life and enslavement. These intersecting histories become the foundation for a personal cosmology, a self-authored science for mapping the spaces where memory, emotion, and ancestry reside. Working with burlap, wood, clay, oil paint, and elemental materials, Flowers builds layered environments in which the ancestral and imagined can coexist.

events.title: AI, Copyright, and Libraries: Guidelines for Faculty, Students, and Researchers
events.description: AI tools offer faculty, students, and researchers an alluring way to locate and synthesize library-licensed materials, but these efficiency gains may not always comply with copyright law, license terms, or research ethics. This session reviews responsible uses of AI with licensed content in the USC Libraries collections. Participants will examine emerging court rulings on copyright and large language models, along with database vendor license requirements. USC librarians Benjamin Hall and Bridgid Fennell will also cover best practices for sharing library resources in Brightspace and introduce AI features in several library databases. The AI, Copyright, and Libraries workshop is presented as part of the USC Center for Excellence in Teaching's fall series.

events.title: Will AI Deepen the Digital Divide in Health Care Systems?
events.description: The AI push in health care systems is underway. Medicare is piloting programs that use AI to authorize care, AI scribes are now a routine part of patient visits, and AI-powered chatbots are being touted as the answer to longstanding therapist shortages. Meanwhile, federal health officials and private companies are promoting AI as the solution to access and care deserts in rural communities, with some of the $50 billion from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program fund fueling the AI expansion effort. But doctors and researchers caution that many of these programs and tools are being rolled out before they’re fully tested for safety, accuracy and fairness. How can AI-powered care respond to patients’ cultural backgrounds with sensitivity and nuance, even as traditional medicine so often falls short? Experts also warn of a new digital divide emerging between large health systems and academic medical centers and safety net systems, with the latter largely excluded from conversations on how AI should be evaluated and monitored. One recent study found that only 44% of hospitals using predictive models evaluated them for bias, and less than two thirds of hospitals using the models tested them for accuracy. That means that some of the country’s most vulnerable patients are likely to bear the brunt of the ongoing experiment of AI in health care. In this webinar, we’ll dive deeper into these trends, highlight story angles to track, and identify questions reporters should be asking about how AI tools are being deployed and whether they risk deepening existing disparities. Leading the conversation are Paige Nong, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Minnesota School of Public Health, and Darius Tahir, a correspondent for KFF Health News who covers health technology. events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: Macdonald expansions of LLT polynomials and the Stanley-Stembridge conjecture
events.description: Anton Mellit, University of Vienna Title: Macdonald expansions of LLT polynomials and the Stanley-Stembridge conjecture Abstract: Recently Hikita proved the Stanley-Stembridge conjecture by constructing an explicit expansion of chromatic quasisymmetric functions in the e-basis, with coefficients products of ratios of q-analogs. I will explain how the chromatic quasisymmetric functions, more precisely their close cousins unicellular LLT (Lascoux-Leclerc-Thibon) polynomials, can be computed using the so-called A_{q,t} algebra, constructed by Carlsson and myself in order to prove the shuffle conjecture. Using the geometric basis constructed subsequently by Carlsson, Gorsky and myself, it is possible to explicitly present the LLTs as linear combinations of modified Macdonald polynomials, and specializing at t=1 we recover Hikita's formula. This is a joint work with Griffin, Romero, Weigl and Wen.

events.title: Mathematical Finance Colloquium: The Mean-Field Limit of Online Stochastic Vector Balancing
events.description: Joe Jackson, University of Chicago [in-person] Title: The Mean-Field Limit of Online Stochastic Vector Balancing Abstract: This talk will be about recent joint work with Christian Fiedler, Daniel Lacker, and Jonathan Niles-Weed, in which we derive a mean-field scaling limit for a class of combinatorial optimization problems. In particular, we study a stochastic online version of the vector balancing problem: n independent standard Gaussian random vectors, each of dimension n, arrive one at a time. The goal is to assign a sign to each vector, based only on the vectors observed so far, so as to minimize the expected maximum norm of the signed sum. Prior work showed that the optimal value is O(sqrt(n)), at least for vectors with independent Rademacher entries, by constructing and analyzing specific algorithms. Our main contribution is to prove that, after rescaling by sqrt(n), it converges to the value of a nonstandard stochastic control problem of mean-field type. events.title: RTG USC Topology Seminar: Functoriality of the L-infinity structure for Legendrian contact homology
events.description: Jason Ma, Duke University Title: Functoriality of the L-infinity structure for Legendrian contact homology Abstract: For any Legendrian knot or link in R^3, L. Ng constructed an L-infinity algebra extending the Chekanov-Eliashberg DGA by combinatorially incorporating information from rational Symplectic Field Theory. We reformulate this L-infinity algebra in terms of disk counts with multiple positive punctures on parallel copies of a Legendrian. This perspective yields a proof of the functoriality of the L-infinity algebra under exact Lagrangian cobordisms. If time permits, we will present some exploratory examples of how this L-infinity structure can be used to define cluster structures on augmentation varieties, and we establish new obstructions to the exact Lagrangian fillability of Legendrian links.

events.title: Algebra Seminar: Bethe algebras for gl(n), tame representations, and a cactus group action
events.description: Iva Halacheva, Northeastern University Title: Bethe algebras for gl(n), tame representations, and a cactus group action Abstract: The Yangian Y(gl(n)) contains a family of maximal commutative subalgebras, known as the Bethe algebras, that generalize the Gelfand-Tsetlin algebras and are indexed by points of the Deligne-Mumford compactification of the moduli space M(0,n+2). We consider points C in the real locus of this parameter space. For a fixed tame representation of Y(gl(n)), the Bethe subalgebra B(C) corresponding to C acts with simple spectrum, resulting in an unramified covering of the parameter space whose fiber over C is the set of eigenlines for the action of B(C). I will discuss how to identify each fiber with a collection of Gelfand-Tsetlin keystone patterns, carrying a gl(n)-crystal structure, as well as the monodromy action for the covering realized by the mirabolic cactus group. This is joint work with Anfisa Gurenkova and Leonid Rybnikov.

events.description: Opening reception: Thursday, November 5, 6 – 9 pm Exhibition on view: November 5 – 20, 2026 Gallery hours: Tuesday – Sunday, 11am – 5pm Roski Graduate Gallery (Los Angeles Arts District) 1262 Palmetto St, Los Angeles, CA 90013 More information here: https://roski.usc.edu/amanda-flowers/ ABOUT THE EXHIBITION Interdisciplinary artist Flowers explores the hidden communication and connection with our living planet through the practice of secret and sacral tools historically used in the preservation of Black ancestral linkage. Moving through an expansive language of identification she implements numerology, metaphysics, and spiritual mythologies, developing her own visual vernacular termed “Leavings.” Cumulatively, her practice embodies a site to dissect the duality of herself, a safe haven to sift through repressed energy. She creates a fragmented code from the threads of primordial dreamscapes to the cosmos, and in so doing a broader consideration of what makes a reflexive state. ABOUT THE ARTIST Amanda Flowers (b. 1995) is an interdisciplinary artist from the Bay Area, based in Los Angeles. Flowers initially attended Arizona State University to study astrophysics before rediscovering her passion for painting and returning home to pursue art in 2015. She later moved to Los Angeles, where she became immersed in the entertainment industry while developing her practice as an emerging artist. In 2023, Flowers received her BA in Studio Art from California State University, Los Angeles. Flowers’s work draws from her dreams, inherited familial memories, and imagined terrains of the “The Shadow Realm.” Her practice is deeply informed by the journey of her maternal grandparents, who migrated from North Carolina during the Great Migration in the late 1960s. Through envisioned ancestral motifs, she creates bridges between generations honoring her lineage. Drawing from a constellation of Black spiritual traditions and mythologies, Flowers moves between the emotional subconscious, the metaphysical and material histories of Black life and enslavement. These intersecting histories become the foundation for a personal cosmology, a self-authored science for mapping the spaces where memory, emotion, and ancestry reside. Working with burlap, wood, clay, oil paint, and elemental materials, Flowers builds layered environments in which the ancestral and imagined can coexist.

events.title: PIPE Workshop: Miriam Venturini (UC Riverside Economics)
events.description: The Imperfect Union: Labor Racketeering, Corruption Exposure, and Its Consequences Can exposing corruption have negative consequences? I tackle this question in the context of labor unions in the U.S., where the U.S. Senate McClellan Committee (1957-1960) publicly exposed corruption and organized crime infiltrations in their ranks. Using a difference-in-differences identification strategy and novel data, I examine the consequences of the Committee’s investigation on unionization, the capacity of unions to mobilize voters during elections, and their ability to influence public policy. I study both the direct effects of the investigation in areas where investigated union locals were present and the indirect effects (or spillovers) in areas where no investigated union locals were present. First, I find that the negative spillover effects on unionization were stronger than the direct effects. Second, I show that the investigation caused a persistent decrease in the capacity of unions to foster voters’ political participation in presidential elections. Finally, I provide evidence suggesting that the spillovers are at least partially explained by a large-scale news and reputation shock that had negative consequences on the entire American labor movement. events.title: EMSI LA2026 "American Landmarks: The Walking Purchase of 1737"
events.description: The American Landmarks series explores historical touchstones in The Huntington’s collections, including objects featured in the “This Land Is…” exhibition, through a mix of panel discussions and community conversations. Join scholars, storytellers, and community experts to excavate the layered histories of this country through these cultural landmarks and discuss the lessons they hold for the present. LA2026 is presented by the USC-Huntington Early Modern Studies Institute. It brings together members of the public and humanities scholars for eighteen conversations about museum and cultural exhibitions at six partnering institutions in the Los Angeles region, including the Autry Museum of the American West, The Huntington, LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes / El El Pueblo de Los Angeles Historical Monument, Mission San Gabriel Arcángel, the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, and USC Libraries. Each exhibition frames conversations about the anniversary of 1776 from the perspective of California and the West. Each discussion will focus on specific items from one of the partner exhibitions, encouraging public discussions about national identities, relationships between regional and national narratives, participating in democracy, and human relationships to the land. The EMSI LA2026 Project has been made possible in part by a major grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities.

events.title: METRANS Seminar: Insights from Analyzing Transport Behavior to Mega-Events in Los Angeles with Large-Scale Human Mobility
events.description: Join the METRANS Transportation Consortium, USC Price School of Public Policy's transportation research center for a seminar with speaker Dr. Abigail Horn, Research Computer Scientist at the Information Sciences Institute and incoming Research Assistant Professor in the Daniel J. Epstein Dept. of Industrial and Systems Engineering. Lunch provided! About the talk: The 2028 Los Angeles Olympics will require innovative transportation strategies to move hundreds of thousands of travelers reliably to and from events. The challenge is that these mega-events produce travel behaviors that differ from routine patterns and which exceed the scope of existing planning models. Large-scale and continuously updated human mobility data from smartphones now enable direct observation of how millions of people adjust their travel in and around major events in high spatial and temporal resolution. This project will leverage large-scale mobile data to build a foundation for modeling mega-event travel and inform innovations in transportation planning models well beyond the Olympics, pioneering adaptations of mobile data that could model travel patterns from novel events such as evacuations or changes to infrastructure to accommodate safety, health, economic, or seasonal needs. About the speaker: Abigail Horn, PhD is a Research Computer Scientist at the Information Sciences Institute and incoming Research Assistant Professor in the Daniel J. Epstein Dept. of Industrial and Systems Engineering in the School of Engineering at the University of Southern California. She was recently a Research Associate in the Dept. of Population and Public Health Sciences, also at USC. The general area of her research is the combination of approaches from network and computational social science and systems modeling with large-scale novel data sources to design solutions to pressing public health challenges. Dr. Horn focuses on problems in food systems and nutrition, and infectious disease modeling.

events.title: Forbidden Pages: Past and Present
events.description: Forbidden Pages: Past and Present features books, periodicals, photographs, and other materials from the USC Libraries’ collections that tell the story of censorship and resistance over the centuries. Among them are a charred fragment of Lion Feuchtwanger’s novel Jud Süß, pulled from the embers of the Nazi book burnings in Berlin in 1933; a 1761 edition of the Catholic Church’s Index Librorum Prohibitorum, its centuries-long list of prohibited books; and a 1954 issue of ONE Magazine which the Los Angeles postmaster declared obscene and refused to mail. Visitors will also encounter works by authors ranging from John Milton, Harriet Beecher Stowe, and Mark Twain to Toni Morrison, Judy Blume, and Salman Rushdie. The exhibition opens on Monday, October 5, in Doheny Memorial Library’s first-floor and runs through the fall semester. Presented in partnership with the USC Open Dialogue Project.

events.description: Kris Cohen is trained as a media theorist and an art historian. These two fields come together in his work on the technological mediation of social life. His first large scale research project, now complete, takes up this history near the end, with the advent of electronic networks and the building of new collective forms in networked environments. Future projects will extend this history back in time as a way to better understand the present. One will consider the relationship between art practices and changes to the intellectual property laws that govern creative labor and the commons. Another seeks to write a history for the bitmap as a mid-century screen technology that significantly transformed techniques of visual representation. Kris' PhD is in Art History from the University of Chicago (2010).

events.title: Amanda Flowers: Cosmic Nexus of The Soul • Soil | MFA Art Solo Thesis Exhibition
events.description: Opening reception: Thursday, November 5, 6 – 9 pm Exhibition on view: November 5 – 20, 2026 Gallery hours: Tuesday – Sunday, 11am – 5pm Roski Graduate Gallery (Los Angeles Arts District) 1262 Palmetto St, Los Angeles, CA 90013 More information here: https://roski.usc.edu/amanda-flowers/ ABOUT THE EXHIBITION Interdisciplinary artist Flowers explores the hidden communication and connection with our living planet through the practice of secret and sacral tools historically used in the preservation of Black ancestral linkage. Moving through an expansive language of identification she implements numerology, metaphysics, and spiritual mythologies, developing her own visual vernacular termed “Leavings.” Cumulatively, her practice embodies a site to dissect the duality of herself, a safe haven to sift through repressed energy. She creates a fragmented code from the threads of primordial dreamscapes to the cosmos, and in so doing a broader consideration of what makes a reflexive state. ABOUT THE ARTIST Amanda Flowers (b. 1995) is an interdisciplinary artist from the Bay Area, based in Los Angeles. Flowers initially attended Arizona State University to study astrophysics before rediscovering her passion for painting and returning home to pursue art in 2015. She later moved to Los Angeles, where she became immersed in the entertainment industry while developing her practice as an emerging artist. In 2023, Flowers received her BA in Studio Art from California State University, Los Angeles. Flowers’s work draws from her dreams, inherited familial memories, and imagined terrains of the “The Shadow Realm.” Her practice is deeply informed by the journey of her maternal grandparents, who migrated from North Carolina during the Great Migration in the late 1960s. Through envisioned ancestral motifs, she creates bridges between generations honoring her lineage. Drawing from a constellation of Black spiritual traditions and mythologies, Flowers moves between the emotional subconscious, the metaphysical and material histories of Black life and enslavement. These intersecting histories become the foundation for a personal cosmology, a self-authored science for mapping the spaces where memory, emotion, and ancestry reside. Working with burlap, wood, clay, oil paint, and elemental materials, Flowers builds layered environments in which the ancestral and imagined can coexist.

events.title: The Missing Middle
events.description: Join exhibition curators Milton S.F. Curry and Valéry Augustin for a thought-provoking conversation exploring the role of housing in shaping the postwar Black middle class and the enduring legacy of architect Paul R. Williams. They will examine how contemporary artists and designers engage with Williams's work, influence, and vision for community-centered architecture. The discussion will feature commissioned artists and architects: EnFOLD Collective (Megan Echols and Dana McKinney White), Janna Ireland, Amanda Williams, and more. This program is presented in collaboration with the USC School of Architecture and USC Fisher Museum of art in conjunction with the exhibition Paul R. Williams: An Architect Considered . About the exhibit: Paul R. Williams: An Architect Considered debuts recently acquired archival drawings, photographs, and plans and pairs them with newly commissioned works by leading contemporary artists, architects, and filmmakers, reframing Paul R Williams’s long under-recognized work and addressing urgent conversations about race, equity, and the future of American cities. A pivotal figure in 20th-century architecture and civil rights advocacy who studied architectural engineering at USC, Williams was the first Black architect licensed west of the Mississippi. He was also the first known Black member of the American Institute of Architects nationwide (1923), its first Black Fellow (1957), and the first and only Black architect to receive its highest honor, the Gold Medal (posthumously, 2017). Over a career spanning nearly six decades, he is estimated to have designed approximately 3,000 structures, making him one of the most prolific and influential architects of his time. Highlighting 31 housing projects from his long career, Paul R. Williams: An Architect Considered spotlights Williams’ innovative solutions for collective living, primarily in Los Angeles, during the second Great Migration, a period of rapid urbanization. More than 60 items from the Paul R. Williams Archive, which was jointly acquired in 2020 by the USC School of Architecture and the Getty Research Institute, will be shown in conversation with major new commissions, as well as a selection of existing works by photographers Julius Shulman and Janna Ireland. Significant support for this exhibition and event has been generously provided by the Mellon Foundation.

events.title: Levan Institute Series: “On Writing”—Paragraphs
events.description: This event is part of the Levan Institute for the Humanities' “On Writing” series, conversations aiming to answer questions about how writing matters, now. This conversation will feature Angelica Jade Bastién (writer, essayist, and film critic) and Anahid Nersessian (UCLA), hosted by Sarah Mesle (USC). Organized in partnership with the Consortium for Gender, Sexuality, Race and Public Culture. Registration is required. REGISTER Description: Prose comes in sentences, and these sentences — almost always — come clustered together into that mysterious unit: “the paragraph.” In elementary school, most of us use a simple spell that can turn a sequence of sentences into a cohesive idea: start with a topic sentence, follow it with a piece of evidence, and wave the magic wand of analysis. Sometimes, the magic works, and the reader finds themselves with a fascinating, cohesive, idea. But for many of us, paragraph magic is more elusive. How much evidence? What counts as analysis? How might the magic of a paragraph be altered by the size of a font, piece of paper, or iPhone screen? What makes a good paragraph in a magazine, an essay, a substack, or an article? In this event, journalist Angelica Jade Bastien will compare paragraph notes with Anahid Nersessian, author and professor of English at UCLA. Angelica Jade Bastién is a writer, film critic, and essayist. She has been on staff at New York Magazine since 2017. She has previously written for The Atlantic, The New York Times, Harper’s Bazaar, The Village Voice, the Criterion Collection and many other publications. She has appeared on podcasts including Blank Check, New York Times’s Cannonball, KCRW’s the Sam Sanders Show, and We Hate Movies. In 2022, she was nominated for a National Magazine Award. She can be found on her Substack newsletter, Madwomen & Muses. Her website is angelicabastien.com. Originally from the South, Bastién now lives in Chicago. Anahid Nersessian was born and raised in New York City. She is the author of three books—Keats's Odes: A Lover's Discourse (Verso, 2022; U of Chicago P, 2021), The Calamity Form: On Poetry and Social Life (Chicago, 2020), and Utopia, Limited: Romanticism and Adjustment (Harvard UP, 2015). Her fourth book, How to Have Sex in a Poem, will be published in 2027 by FSG. Her work has appeared in The New Yorker, The New York Review of Books, The London Review of Books, New Left Review, n+1, The Los Angeles Review of Books, The Paris Review, Bidoun, Poetry Magazine, Mousse, e-flux, and elsewhere. She lives in Los Angeles, where she is a professor in the Department of English at UCLA. Open to attendants outside of USC. Registration before the event is required. To see more events in this series, including recordings of past events, visit https://dornsife.usc.edu/levan-institute/programs/on-writing/.

events.title: VSRI Lecture by Molly Kalkstein
events.description: Competing ideas about whether photography is a medium of interchangeable duplicates or of valuable originals have circulated throughout its history, but never did they have such tangible repercussions as during and in the immediate aftermath of the so-called “photo boom” of the 1970s. At the core of this boom was the emergence of a robust market heralding an unprecedented rise in prices and status for photographic prints. This presentation will examine and contextualize the professional practices, public discourses, and shifts in language that underpinned the repositioning of photography as a fine art collectible, considering ways that developments during this period exerted an outsized influence on the study, exhibition, and valuation of photographs—one that continues to resonate through the present day.

events.title: Landmarks in Japanese Warrior Law, Part 2: Nishita Tomohiro on the "Mirror of the East"
events.description: This is Part 2 of a two-part webinar series exploring the development of warrior law during Japan’s Kamakura period through two foundational texts. More information will be available soon. These lectures will be presented in Japanese. English translations of the full talks will be available, and interpretation will be provided during the Q&A. Questions in English and Japanese are welcome. Register for the webinar series here. Webinar 1 Friday, Nov. 13 | 3–5 PM How Did the 1232 Formulary (Goseibai shikimoku) Become the Celebrity of Kamakura Legal Sources? Lecture by Yuki Satō, Rikkyo University Webinar 2 Friday, Nov. 20 | 3–5 PM Warrior Law After 1232: Supplementary Lawmaking in the Mirror of the East (Azuma kagami) Lecture by Nishita Tomohiro, Historiographical Institute at the University of Tokyo About the Speakers Tomohiro Nishita (Historiographical Institute, University of Tokyo) 佐藤雄基（立教大学） Nishita Tomohiro is Associate Professor at the Historiographical Institute at the University of Tokyo. He specializes in research on medieval policing and criminal investigatory powers, as well as social structures. He graduated from the Department of History and Culture in the Faculty of Letters at the University of Tokyo and then withdrew from the Ph.D. program at the University of Tokyo Graduate School of Humanities and Sociology, Socio-cultural Studies division. He now holds a Ph.D. in literature. He joined the Historiographical Institute as a research assistant, and then became assistant professor, and now associate professor in the medieval materials department. Notable works include a modern-Japanese translation of the Azuma kagami (Mirror of the East) in 16 volumes, Akuto Meshitori no Chusei (Medieval Japan’s Cackdown on Banditry, 2017), Shoen no shikumi to Kurashi (The Structure and Daily Life of Landed Estates, 2021), and Japanese Classics for Beginners: Azuma kagami in 2021. Yuki Satō (Rikkyo University) 佐藤雄基（立教大学） Yuki Satō is Professor of History at Rikkyo University in Tokyo, Japan. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Tokyo in 2011. His primary areas of expertise are diplomatics (paleography) and the legal and social history of early medieval Japan (11th–14th centuries). His notable works include Chusei-shoki no Monjo to Soshō (Early Medieval Documents and Lawsuits in Japan, 2012) and Goseibai-shikimoku: Kamakura Bushi no Hō to Seikatsu (Japanese First Samurai Code of Law: The Legal Life of Kamakura Warriors, 2023). Discussant Kiyoshi Jinno (Tokyo University of Science) 神野潔（東京理科大学） Kiyoshi Jinno is Professor at the Institute of Arts and Sciences at Tokyo University of Science. His areas of expertise include the legal history of medieval Japan and the history of legal thought in modern Japan. His publications include The Handbook of the Goseibai Shikimoku (2024) and Outline of Japanese Legal History (2022). He is currently researching the law and judiciary of the Kamakura shogunate and the history of legal studies in modern Japan. This webinar series is co-presented by the Yanai Initiative.

Bios: Gautam Rangan is a Los Angeles–based multidisciplinary artist working at the intersection of technology, perception, and environmental storytelling. Using projection mapping, interactive systems, and spatial design, he creates immersive installations that examine relationships between body, language, and place. Drawing on backgrounds in engineering, design, and large-scale experiential environments, he has contributed to public, commercial, and cultural projects for global audiences. Since 2020, his independent artistic practice has focused on installation as a medium for perceptual inquiry. Recent works, including Light Unshapes, investigate optical illusion, sensory instability, and the fluid relationship between form and flow. @gautam_rangan Neelanjana Banerjee is a writer whose fiction, poetry, and essays have appeared widely in journals and anthologies like Prairie Schooner, Weird Sister, Virginia Quarterly Review, PANK Magazine, The Rumpus, and many other places. She is a co-editor of Indivisible: An Anthology of Contemporary South Asian American Poetry and The Coiled Serpent: Poets Arising from the Cultural Quakes and Shifts of Los Angeles. Her journalism has appeared on Teen Vogue, The Aerogram, The Center for Asian American Media Blog, LA Review of Books, Alternet, WordRiot, Colorlines, Fiction Writers Review, and more. She is based in Los Angeles, where she is the Managing Editor of Kaya Press, and teaches writing and publishing in the Asian American Studies Department at UCLA and through private writing workshops. Devavani Chatterjea (she/they) is a Bengali American scientist, educator, writer, and policymaker whose work explores the connections between bodies, environments, and health. An empaneled artist of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations, she has served as a panelist for the National Endowment for the Arts, California Arts Council, and World Arts West. events.title: Carlee Nixon: From Me For You
events.description: Opening Reception: Wednesday, November 18, 5–7pm ARTIST STATEMENT: “From Me For You” examines privacy as a fragile and socially constructed boundary between the self and an external gaze. Through scale, proximity, and perspective, I invite viewers into otherwise inaccessible spaces of personal moments of the body, positioning them as voyeurs of mundane, still moments. By making an ordinary subject the focus, I question the conditions under which looking becomes an act of invasion and objectification, and how visibility complicates our expectations of control, consent, and privacy. events.title: Chloe Smalls Johnson: Point of No Return
events.description: Opening Reception: Wednesday, November 18, 5–7pm ARTIST STATEMENT: "Point of No Return" explores the surrounding textural and ecological environment of South Central LA, reasoning through the explored sites through "textural digestion" and psychogeography, which describes the effect of a geographical location on the emotions and even behavior of individuals. Connections between human adaptation and botanical adaptation inspires the themes around our relationships with the built and ecological environment, focusing on how ecological inequity in the area affects the way humans interact with and relate to their communities. Processes of collection, multi-media collage, and layering mirrors her own experience navigating the landscape through layers of anecdotal experiences that intersect with learned histories about the area to form an alternative site study. events.title: Transcultural Mediation in the Early Modern Pacific (California, China, Mexico, Korea, and the Marianas): Classicisms, Canons, and the East-West Journey of Knowledge
events.description: Bringing together scholars from Southern California, China, Korea, the UK, and Guam, this conference explores cultural mediation and East–West encounters in the early modern Pacific. Through the lives and intellectual pursuits of Western missionaries and the work of Chinese and Korean intellectuals, we examine how knowledge moved across cultures in this age of global convergence. Special attention goes to antiquities and canons, including how Greco-Roman antiquity shaped European views of China and helped introduce European culture to late Ming audiences. The conference also considers the tension between the creation of global narratives and the attention to indigenous identities and local perspectives. The conference is sponsored by the Department of Classics, the Levan Institute for the Humanities, the Center for the Premodern World, the School of Religion, the Institute for Advanced Catholic Studies, the Department of East Asian Languages and Culture, the Early Modern Studies Institute, and Nova Forum.

events.title: Levan Book Chat—Jonathan Leal, Wild Tongue
events.description: A discussion of Jonathan Leal's new book, Wild Tongue: A Borderlands Mixtape (Duke University Press, 2026). The author will be joined in conversation by Alex E. Chávez (University of Notre Dame) and Richard T. Rodriguez (UC Riverside), moderated by Edwin Hill (USC). Organized in partnership with the Department of English, Experimental Humanities Lab, and Center for Music, Brain and Society. Registration is required. REGISTER HERE About the Book: In Wild Tongue, writer, scholar, and musician Jonathan Leal invites readers to the Texas borderlands to witness contemporary sonic cultures and expressive forms of Latine struggle and world-making. Blending autoethnography, music criticism, and border theory into an epistolary mixtape, Leal depicts the borderlands as a generative place made by its inhabitants, a geography where creativity and cultural performance engage powerfully with politico-aesthetic issues, create communal identity, and challenge xenophobic and nationalist dominance. Across the mixtape’s contrasting “tracks,” Leal situates living artistries within longer, local arcs of borderlands creativity, amplifying Gloria Anzaldúa’s durable, pathbreaking observation, “Wild tongues can’t be tamed, they can only be cut out.” Combining lyric nonfiction, artist interviews, archival research, transdisciplinary analysis, and popular music criticism and production, Wild Tongue presents an exhilarating, embracing account of freedoms pursued between worlds. About the Author: Jonathan Leal is Associate Professor of English and Affiliated Faculty in the Thornton School of Music at the University of Southern California. He is the author of Dreams in Double Time: On Race, Freedom, and Bebop, also published by Duke University Press, and coeditor of Cybermedia: Explorations in Science, Sound, and Vision. Open to attendants outside of USC. An excerpt of the book will be made available to registered attendants. Registration before the event is required. This event is part of the Levan Institute for the Humanities' “Book Chats” series, conversations about new books published by USC scholars in the humanities and humanistic social sciences. To see more events in this series, including recordings of past events, visit https://dornsife.usc.edu/levan-institute/book-chats/.

events.title: Experience L.A.: Oh, Mary! at the Ahmanson Theatre
events.description: ADMISSION: Admission is free and open to current USC students only, who must use the provided transportation to attend. Space is limited and advance registration is required. RSVP beginning Monday, November 2, at 10 a.m. RSVP Tickets will be distributed at check-in on the day of the event. Check-in for the event will begin at 5:45 p.m. on campus. Buses will depart at 6:30 p.m. and return to campus at 9:45 p.m. Dinner will be provided. DESCRIPTION: Oh, Mary! Written by Cole Escola Directed by Sam Pinkleton "80 minutes of almost uninterrupted laughter. A work of genius."–The Hollywood Reporter The Tony Award–Winning and Pulitzer Prize finalist hit comedy makes its Los Angeles premiere! USC students will have the opportunity to catch Oh, Mary!, a dark comedy about a miserable, suffocated Mary Todd Lincoln in the weeks leading up to Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. Unrequited yearning, alcoholism, and suppressed desires abound in this 80-minute play that finally examines the forgotten life and dreams of Mrs. Lincoln through the lens of an idiot (playwright Cole Escola). Declared "one of the best comedies in years" by The New York Times, Oh, Mary! received two Tony Awards, including Best Direction of a Play (Sam Pinkleton), Drama League Awards for Outstanding Play and Outstanding Direction of a Play, as well as a special citation from the New York Drama Critics’ Circle. It was named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Oh, Mary! runs at the Ahmanson Theatre from November 10 to December 6, 2026. To attend on your own and purchase tickets, visit http://centertheatregroup.org. Presented by USC Visions and Voices.

events.title: METRANS Seminar- Making Rural Transit Work: New Models for Better Access
events.description: Join the METRANS Transportation Consortium, USC Price School of Public Policy's transportation research center for a seminar with speakr Dr. John Carlsson, Associate Professor at the University of Southern California in the Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering. Lunch provided! About the talk: Rural transit systems face unique constraints in connecting dispersed population centers while maintaining economic viability, which necessitates a modelling approach that addresses multiple competing objectives simultaneously. However, very little research has been conducted on the application of continuous approximation models to problems in rural transit networks, likely due to their distinctive spatial characteristics and coverage requirements. The purpose of this project is to discover new continuous approximation models for public transit network design, with a specific focus on rural areas. This project will combine tools from geospatial optimization, computational geometry, and geometric probability theory to formulate new models. Furthermore, these models will identify which complementary infrastructure investments would most effectively increase transit availability and ridership in rural counties. About the speaker: John Carlsson, PhD is an Associate Professor at the University of Southern California in the Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering. He received his Ph.D. from the Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineeering (ICME) at Stanford University and his A.B. in mathematics and music from Harvard College. He works on algorithms for solving problems in continuous location theory, and more generally, optimization problems that have some kind of geographic element. His research is currently supported by DARPA, the Office of Naval Research, the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, the National Science Foundation, and the Minnesota Department of Transportation (MnDOT).

events.title: Racist by Design: In Conversation with Kelly Lytle Hernández & Bill Deverell
events.description: ICW is proud to present Dr. Kelly Lytle Hernández, Professor of History, African American Studies, and Urban Planning at UCLA, in conversation with Bill Deverell about her new book, Racist by Design. Drawing on decades of historical research, Lytle Hernández reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcement officials deliberately shaped the U.S. immigration system to encourage white immigration while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, criminalization, and deportation. Exposing the racial foundations of immigration policy and its enduring consequences, this conversation will dive into the immigration system’s origins and how we might reimagine its future. Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), andBad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based, community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative’s principal advisor. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández was named a 2019MacArthur “Genius” Fellow. She is also a past president of the Western History Association, president-elect of the Society of American Historians, and an elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board.

events.title: Make Mend III: Simple Construction, Etui, and Put a Pocket on It
events.description: ADMISSION: Admission is free and open to everyone. Reservations required. RSVP beginning Monday, November 2, at 10 a.m. RSVP DESCRIPTION: Make Mend returns for its third iteration at USC! Organized by the USC Roski School of Art and Design, this ongoing series of workshops and craft events focuses on sustainability, repair, and creative reuse. In this first workshop, participants learn introductory techniques, including how to make their own pincushions and small cases. The series welcomes participants of all experience levels. No previous sewing or construction experience is required, and tools and materials will be provided. What to Expect Learn simple hand-sewing and construction techniques using repurposed fabrics. Participants may move among several hands-on activity stations, including: > Pincushion and etui making > Patch and detachable-pocket construction > Visible mending and decorative repair > A communal mending circle > Fabric embellishment using buttons, trims, and handmade notions An etui is a small case designed to hold essential sewing or craft tools. You’ll be invited to create a personal etui or pincushion! This is One Part of a Series! Make Mend III is a three-part participatory series exploring handwork, material experimentation, sustainability, and community exchange. Each event stands on its own, so you're welcome to join us for any or all of the three workshops. Across the series, participants can learn practical techniques, experiment with natural materials, and explore how making and mending can extend the life of objects while creating opportunities for creativity and connection. Make Mend III: Open Vat Friday, February 5, 2027, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Watt Hall South Lawn Make Mend III: Work + Artist/Crafter Barter Fair Friday, April 2, 2027, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sunken Lawn south of Watt Hall and Watt Hall Courtyard Presented by USC Visions and Voices and the USC Roski School of Art and Design.

events.title: EMSI LA2026 “Historical Memory, Federal Agencies, Mission Conservation”
events.description: A virtual conversation with Yve Chavez (Associate Professor of Art History, University of Oklahoma) and Sarah Montoya (Co-Director, Indigenous Humanities Lab, Virginia Commonwealth University), moderated by Julia Lewandoski (Assistant Professor of History, University of California, San Diego). Panelists will consider Indigenous responses to Spanish colonial heritage in California, including public art, national trails, and historic sites. LA2026 is presented by the USC-Huntington Early Modern Studies Institute. It brings together members of the public and humanities scholars for eighteen conversations about museum and cultural exhibitions at six partnering institutions in the Los Angeles region, including the Autry Museum of the American West, The Huntington, LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes / El El Pueblo de Los Angeles Historical Monument, Mission San Gabriel Arcángel, the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, and USC Libraries. Each exhibition frames conversations about the anniversary of 1776 from the perspective of California and the West. Each discussion will focus on specific items from one of the partner exhibitions, encouraging public discussions about national identities, relationships between regional and national narratives, participating in democracy, and human relationships to the land. The EMSI LA2026 Project has been made possible in part by a major grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities.

events.title: Workshop@PAM: Circulating Knowledge Through the Air and Land
events.description: Workshop: Circulating Knowledge Through Air and Land Synthetic prayer flags have been enthusiastically embraced throughout the Himalayas and by Buddhist communities around the world over the last three decades. Traditionally, prayer flags, known as lungta and tarchod, were intended to carry prayers and blessings on the wind and were printed as needed in villages and monasteries using biodegradable materials. Mass production using synthetic fabrics and screen printing has made prayer flags more convenient to obtain. However, the discovery of microplastics in high mountain environments, along with growing concerns about waste in glaciers, streams, and the stomachs of nonhuman animals, has led communities to critically reconsider whether this convenience is worth the environmental impact. How can prayer flags once again foster good relationships between humans, the land, and more-than-human beings? This workshop will guide participants in creating prayer flags using ancestral knowledge from the Himalayas while exploring the interconnected issues of Indigenous knowledge, sustainability, and waste in global ecosystems. USC staff and students, as well as PAM members, receive a 20% discount. Please email info@pam.usc.edu for the discount code or additional information. Tickets include museum admission toWe Are Connected, and parking. More about Dr. Kalzang Dorjee Bhutia: Kalzang Dorjee Bhutia is a scholar from the Lhopo community in the Sikkim Himalayas. He has published and taught extensively on Indigenous knowledge, Buddhism, the environment, and the return and repair of local knowledge and histories in the mountains. He has made traditional prayer flags since childhood and now shares this knowledge with local communities throughout the Himalayas. This program is presented in conjunction with two current exhibitions: Gateway to Himalayan Art, a traveling exhibition organized and provided by the Rubin Museum of Himalayan Art, and We Are Connected: Highlights from the USC Pacific Asia Museum’s Himalayan Collection.

events.title: Film Screening - "The Mochi Movie"
events.description: Join the USC Shinso Ito Center for Japanese Religions and Culture for a screening of The Mochi Movie, an award-winning documentary that explores the centuries-old Japanese tradition of Mochi-tsuki—the ceremonial pounding of rice to make mochi for the New Year—as a lens into resilience, identity, and intergenerational connection. Set against the backdrop of Japanese American history, including the impact of incarceration during World War II, the film weaves together personal stories, vibrant celebrations, and historical insights. Featuring appearances by cultural icon George Takei, Kristen Hayashi curator at the Japanese American National Museum, and the story of renowned photographer Toyo Miyatake, The Mochi Movie brings together voices across generations to reflect on the deeper meaning of tradition. The film reminds us that traditions matter—not just for preserving the past, but for shaping who we become. Following the screening, attendees will have the opportunity to join a conversation with special guests (to be announced) and enjoy mochi from the historic Los Angeles confectionery Fugetsu-Do. events.title: Michelle Liu Carriger - "An Art of Tea? The Japanese Way of Tea in Contemporary Installation and Performance Art"
events.description: Chanoyu, Japanese “tea ceremony,” has remained a niche, rarified, and arcane practice in the 21st century, even as matcha, the tea form it preserved for centuries, has become a worldwide fad. Meanwhile, a number of artists, both Japanese and not, have found the aesthetics and gestures of chanoyu compelling for adoption into installation and performance art contexts, with or without matcha. Using examples from Japan, the USA, Australia, and Brazil, I ask: What does recourse to a traditional form do for contemporary artists? How do the arcane, specialized gestures learned by practitioners translate—or not—from tatami to the gallery? Artists include fine and performance artists who adapt chanoyu aesthetics, as well as tea practitioners who have experimented with more gallery- and art-focused presentations in distinction to traditional practice: Mariko Mori, Tom Sachs, Matthew Barney, Yumi Umiumare (a Dairakudan Butoh alumna now based in Australia), Maho Ogawa (NYC choreographer), Adam Wojcinski (Australia/France), Sōryō Matsumura (Shuhally studio, Tokyo), Izumi Reijiro (grandson of the 15th-generation Urasenke iemoto and scion of Sabie, a series of modernized tea events in public and private venues), and Erika Kobayashi (Brazil). This event is part of the Ito Center's Japanese Food Culture and Culinary Traditions Speaker Series RSVP About the Speaker Michelle Liu Carriger is an associate professor of Theater and Performance Studies at UCLA with a PhD from Brown University. Her first book, Theatricality of the Closet: Fashion, Performance and Subjectivity Between Victorian Britain and Meiji Japan (2023), was the winner of the Barnard Hewitt Award from ASTR (American Society for Theatre Research). Other publications consider pedagogy during wildfire and active-shooter lockdown, Japanese street fashion, cheerleaders in musicals, Victorian sex scandals, historical reenactment, kimono, and cultural appropriation. A longtime practitioner of chanoyu (“Japanese tea ceremony”) with the tea name (chamei) Sōmi, Michelle’s current book project analyzes tea practice in international circulation, from which this talk’s materials are drawn.\

events.title: Levan Book Chat—Steven J. Ross, The Secret War Against Hate
events.description: A discussion of Steven J. Ross's new book, The Secret War Against Hate: American Resistance to Antisemitism and White Supremacy (Bloomsbury, 2026). The author will be joined in conversation by Steven Hahn (NYU) and Michael Kazin (Georgetown University), moderated by Alaina Morgan (USC). Registration is required. REGISTER HERE About the Book: Americans today like to believe that the end of World War II brought a new era of tolerance in the United States. But antisemitism and racism went up-not down-after the war's end. Violence broke out in cities across the country, and the number of organized hate groups more than doubled from 1940 to 1946. In this shocking account of a resurgence of White Supremacy in America, celebrated historian Steven J. Ross reveals how four key leaders-Emory Burke, J. B. Stoner, James Madole, and George Lincoln Rockwell-worked together to “finish the job Hitler had begun,” launching deadly attacks on Jews and African Americans and building a network of terrorists across the U.S. In response to this “war of hate,” three men-Arnold Forster of the Anti-­Defamation League, George Mintzer of the American Jewish Committee, and James Sheldon of the Non-­Sectarian Anti­-Nazi League-along with dozens of men and women, launched a multipronged effort: They infiltrated, monitored, and undermined these hate groups, putting their own safety on the line and scoring important victories that, today, have been all but forgotten. Tracing the extraordinary work of these unsung heroes, The Secret War Against Hate provides a groundbreaking reconsideration of the legacy of the “Good War,” and essential reading on how America today can beat hate once again and build a just and united nation. About the Author: Steven J. Ross is Distinguished Professor of History, Dean’s Professor of History, and Marion and Myron Casden Director of the Casden Institute for the Study of the Jewish Role in American Life. He has written extensively in the areas of working-class history, social history, film history, and political history. He is the author of Workers On the Edge: Work, Leisure, and Politics in Industrializing Cincinnati, 1788-1890 (1985), Working-Class Hollywood: Silent Film and the Shaping of Class in America (1998), Hollywood Left and Right: How Movie Stars Shaped American Politics (2011), and Hitler in Los Angeles: How Jews Foiled Nazi Plots Against Hollywoodand America (2018). Open to attendants outside of USC. An excerpt of the book will be made available to registered attendants. Registration before the event is required. events.description: ADMISSION: Admission is free and open to everyone. Reservations required. RSVP beginning Monday, January 4, at 10 a.m. DESCRIPTION: How do medical dramas shape the way we understand illness and patient care? Through clips, conversation, and firsthand perspectives, this engaging program brings together clinicians, television writers, actors, and disability justice advocates to examine how shows such as The Pitt, The Good Doctor, and Chicago Med influence public attitudes toward health and access. Explore the power of storytelling to build empathy, challenge assumptions, and spark conversations about the realities of living with illness and navigating the health care system. This Is One Part of a Series! This conversation is a part of “As Seen on TV”: Medical Education, Entertainment, and the Reality of Healthcare, a Medical Humanities, Arts, and Ethics event series exploring how medical shows have captivated audiences and shaped our understanding of health care, illness, and the people who provide care. Related Event: The Pitt: Medical Drama and Clinical Reality Monday, February 8, at 12 p.m. Mayer Auditorium, Health Sciences Campus More info and RSVP Speaker Bios: Adam Scott Weissman is a writer, producer, educator, and USC alumnus whose credits include The Good Doctor, where he spent five seasons and finished as co-producer, and episodes of CSI: NY and Proven Innocent. He has also developed television pilots and award-winning stage work. Weissman teaches in USC’s John Wells Division of Writing for Screen & Television and has led creative writing programs for incarcerated and formerly incarcerated writers throughout Los Angeles. Kate Folb is Director and Principal Investigator of Hollywood, Health & Society at the USC Annenberg Norman Lear Center. For more than 20 years, she has worked at the intersection of entertainment and public health, collaborating with television and film creators on issues including substance use, reproductive health, and adolescent well-being. Prior to joining USC, she led entertainment education initiatives for organizations including the Kaiser Family Foundation, Planned Parenthood Federation of America, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. Folb holds degrees from the University of Denver and UCLA. Presented by USC Visions and Voices.
